name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The research firm's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders - the closest thing to sector-wide survey data.
points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

points.desc: Used by thousands of US churches, Gloo surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry - a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations.
points.name: Gloo is the sector's tech platform

points.desc: The interfaith nonprofit network brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together on the ethical deployment of AI in religious contexts.
points.name: AI and Faith convenes the ethics work

points.desc: The university's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life.
points.name: Notre Dame studies AI and human formation

points.desc: The Hartford Institute for Religion Research regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship.
points.name: Hartford surveys congregational technology

points.desc: Pew Research Center's Religion & Public Life work periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces.
points.name: Pew measures public and clergy attitudes

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey places religious organisations within the broader "Other services" category under NAICS 81, where 11.3 percent of firms reported using AI in the most recent period, down slightly from 11.6 percent in the prior period. This is the only official measured figure available, and because it pools religious organisations with other service businesses in the same code, it should be read as indicative rather than precise for congregations alone.

On the deployment side, Gloo describes itself as a platform used by thousands of US churches and offers what it calls values-aligned AI models, developer tools, and benchmarks specifically built for faith-based organisations. Its infrastructure covers inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows, and it frames its offering around unifying siloed congregational data to support what it calls ministry intelligence and next-generation ministry workflows. The platform also maintains an evaluation framework it describes as measuring AI alignment across seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing, an unusual design constraint that reflects the sector's distinctive values pressures.

Research and survey infrastructure for the sector is spread across several organisations. The Barna Group tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders through its State of the Church work. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research has a longer history of surveying congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship. Pew Research Center's Religion and Public Life programme periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology, though the excerpts available here do not report specific AI-related figures from any of these three organisations.

The ethical dimension is unusually prominent in this sector compared with most industries. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit, brings together technologists, scholars, and clergy specifically to apply what it describes as time-tested, faith-based values to the ethical AI conversation, noting that for 85 percent of the world's population who claim a religious affiliation these questions carry spiritual as well as moral weight. The University of Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds research on AI and religious life, and a Notre Dame professor leading that work has stated that using AI to draft anything spoken in worship reflects a basic misunderstanding of what Christians believe is happening when a preacher delivers a homily, a pointed caution about where automation meets sacramental function.

The papal dimension has also entered the picture. Notre Dame's Meghan Sullivan notes that Pope Leo XIV has already signalled he would devote substantial attention to AI challenges, drawing a deliberate parallel to Pope Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical on the Industrial Revolution, and that his recent teaching on the subject, Magnifica humanitas, represents a significant doctrinal statement whose practical reach is now the central challenge.

For a congregation or faith organisation considering deployment, the sector's sourced evidence points to a modest but real level of adoption, a specialist vendor in Gloo offering purpose-built tooling, active research bodies tracking how clergy and congregants respond, and an unusually well-developed ethical conversation cautioning that certain uses, particularly those touching on preaching and pastoral care, carry theological objections that go beyond ordinary change-management concerns. Organisations would be well served by engaging that ethics literature before scoping any project that touches worship or pastoral practice.
